practice.title: From Correct Belief to Valid Cognizer
agreedSteps: Choose one of the sixteen positive conceptions to work on over the next two weeks and try to move from a correct belief to a valid cognizer — an incontrovertible understanding that won't degrade and will actively oppose the wrong conception.

Use the twelve commitments of going for refuge (three abandonments, three acknowledgements, six general commitments) as scaffolding for developing that chosen conception. Funnel the commitments toward the specific change we're working on.
Remember Buddha in everything we do — a simple, profound way to create uncontaminated virtue even without perfect renunciation or bodhichitta.
steps: Check in with ourselves on a three-to-six-month basis: have I become more of an inner being? Am I looking for happiness from within more or less? This is a kind, non-judgmental self-assessment to get clarity on the direction of our spiritual path.

When eating or drinking, pause to remember the Three Jewels and their kindness — igniting our faith many times throughout the day. If practicing tantra, this flows naturally into the yoga of eating: offering to ourselves as Vajrayogini or to our Guru at our heart.
When wishing others well, use the trick of wishing a loved one had the specific Dharma realization we're working on. This compassionate wish often loops back and strengthens our own aspiration.
practice.quote: Would I describe myself as an inner being? We find our happiness from within and we find our freedom from suffering from within. That's what an inner being is.

commentary.title: Sixteen Conceptions as Spiritual Checkpoints
content: Before diving into the MTB text, KK introduced a framework from How to Understand the Mind (page 177) that structured the entire class: the sixteen correct conceptual thoughts and their opposing wrong awarenesses. These are practical, approachable checkpoints on the spiritual path — markers we can aim for before the high realizations of the Five Mahayana Paths.

The idea is that on a spiritual journey, we don't want to take one step forward and one step back. Instead, we want to develop incontrovertible understandings. Buddha explains this as moving from not understanding a Dharma object (or having an absolutely wrong understanding) to developing a correct belief, and then turning that into a valid cognizer — a direct understanding that is proven in our mind. When we can do this, our mind will hold these realizations and they won't degrade.

The sixteen positive conceptions include: remembering death, wishing to take the real meaning of our precious human life, relying faithfully upon our spiritual guide, not being attached to this life's pleasures, fearing lower rebirth, wishing to go for refuge, having faith in karma, seeking virtuous actions, regarding samsara as suffering, wishing to abandon delusions, being determined to attain liberation, wanting to practice the Three Higher Trainings, cherishing all beings, forsaking self-cherishing, realizing selflessness, and liking the practice of secret mantra.
Rather than treating these as abstract ideals, KK encouraged each student to choose one or two as a personal focus and then funnel the refuge commitments toward developing that specific realization.

commentary.title: The Measurement of Going for Refuge
content: The true taking of refuge depends on clearly recognizing the two causes: heartfelt dread of samsaric suffering, and unshakable conviction in the Three Jewels. When we cultivate both sincerely and consistently and place our full reliance upon Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, this is the actual going for refuge.

commentary.title: Commitments: The Three Abandonments
content: Having taken refuge in the Buddha Jewel, we should abandon going for refuge to teachers who contradict Buddha's view or to samsaric gods. Having taken refuge in Dharma, we should abandon harming others. Having taken refuge in Sangha, we should not allow ourselves to be influenced by people who reject Buddha's teachings.

KK showed how each abandonment can be targeted at whichever of the sixteen conceptions we're developing. For example, with conviction in karma: we stop relying on thinkers whose philosophy is really about finding happiness in samsara. We abandon harming others because we're trying to increase our belief in the law of karma. We resist the subtle influence of people who, even with good intentions, attribute their suffering to external causes rather than karma.

The third abandonment is especially subtle. It's not about someone explicitly rejecting Buddhism — it's about the casual influence of friends, family, and cultural voices that lead us away from Dharma understanding. How often do we agree when someone blames their unhappiness on something that happened twenty years ago? From Buddha's view, that's completely wrong — it's their karma. Every bad thing that happens in the world is because of the karma of the people experiencing it. We can still say that something is harmful, but we need to make sure we're not developing a philosophical view that blames the outer person.

commentary.title: Commitments: The Three Acknowledgements and Pure View
content: We should regard any image of Buddha as an actual Buddha, any Dharma scripture as actual Buddha's speech, and anyone wearing ordination robes as actual Sangha. These are practices in pure view — and they lead directly into tantra.

Fran observed that seeing a Buddha image as actual Buddha connects to conviction in karma: it's my karma to be in the presence of a living Buddha. Past me did something really cool to make this incredibly rare appearance happen. David noted that holding pure view of someone in robes is essentially a tantric practice — and that doing it might help you like the practice of secret mantra.

KK confirmed that all three acknowledgements are leading us into pure view from day one of receiving refuge vows. Buddha is teaching people how to enter tantra right away, even within sutra. Mimi added that when seeing a Buddha image, we can also think about our own potential as a future Buddha, which supports meditations on precious human life and selflessness.

As an example of the power of Sangha Jewel practice, KK shared the story of Gen Tarchen, one of Geshe-la's first Western disciples, who had just died. Before ordination his name was Chip — a carpenter and composer who became a monk and then helped establish Manjushri Centre and Tara Centre in Scotland. He participated in Geshe-la's three-year retreat, taught in Toronto (where two people became monks after their very first class with him in 1992), and helped shape many of the tradition's most senior teachers. His impact flowed from strong concentration, deep faith, and experience of Dharma — just one person's example showing the ripple effect of genuine practice.

commentary.title: The Six General Commitments
content: Six commitments to be borne in mind throughout life, each designed to enhance beneficial attitudes and maintain the liberating thought of refuge: (1) Go for refuge again and again, remembering the Three Jewels' qualities; (2) offer the first portion of food and drink to the Three Jewels; (3) with compassion, encourage others to go for refuge; (4) go for refuge at least three times during the day and night; (5) perform every action with complete trust in the Three Jewels; (6) never forsake the Three Jewels, even at the cost of our life or as a joke.

These commitments scale endlessly. They never go dry — they just keep getting richer throughout our whole Dharma career. Each one can be funneled toward whichever conception we're developing. Offering food to the Three Jewels, for example, means pausing each time we eat or drink to ignite our faith. Since we eat and drink constantly, this alone creates many moments of mindfulness each day.

The third commitment — encouraging others to go for refuge — doubles as a compassion practice and a trick for deepening our own realization. When we wish a loved one had a particular Dharma insight (like moral clarity about karma), that compassionate wish often loops back to strengthen our own aspiration. Sometimes we're better at wishing things for others than for ourselves.
KK noted that the practice of refuge is so vast that Atisha, when he came to Tibet and taught extensively on it, was jokingly nicknamed the 'Refuge Lama' — and was pleased by the title.

commentary.title: The Eight Benefits of Going for Refuge
content: KK offered the mnemonic P-E-P-A-H-P-U-Q ('Peppa Pug'): (P) we become a pure Buddhist or inner being, (E) we establish the foundation for all other vows, (P) we purify past negative karma, (A) we daily accumulate vast merit, (H) we are held back from lower rebirths, (P) we are protected from harm by humans and non-humans, (U) we fulfill all temporary and ultimate wishes, (Q) we quickly attain full enlightenment.

Inner being is a beautiful synonym for Buddhist. It means finding happiness from within and finding freedom from suffering from within. KK suggested this as a simple self-assessment: over the last several months, have I become more of an inner being or less? Am I looking for happiness from within more or less? This isn't asked out of perfectionism or self-attack — just kindness, to get clarity on the direction of our path.

commentary.title: Contaminated vs. Uncontaminated Virtue
content: Contaminated virtue is a virtuous action not performed with renunciation, bodhichitta, or a realization of emptiness. It creates good conditions within samsara but doesn't lead to liberation. Uncontaminated virtue requires one of those three minds as its motivation.

However, there is another way to create uncontaminated virtue: performing any action while remembering Buddha, or in relationship to Buddha, because Buddha is outside samsara. This is a simple but profound application of refuge in daily life.

commentary.title: Offering Food to Vajrayogini
content: Mimi asked whether offering the first portion of food to Vajrayogini counts the same as offering to the Three Jewels. KK confirmed: the refuge commitments flow naturally into tantric practice. In Vajrayogini practice, the yoga of eating appears in three of the eleven yogas — the yoga of the Guru, purifying nectar, and daily actions. Rather than eating in a complicated way with a long meditation, practitioners can offer food to themselves as Vajrayogini or to their Guru at their heart as Vajrayogini Heruka.
All the sutra and tantra combines like this. Over time we see they're leading to the exact same place and are mutually supportive.

commentary.title: Hinayana and Mahayana Mindsets: Palace vs. Shack
content: Prompted by Sumit's question about why the Hinayana and Mahayana paths differ, KK explained that the Hinayana mindset thinks full enlightenment is too big a deal. Its approach is to focus narrowly on the Three Higher Trainings to quickly realize emptiness and end suffering — often avoiding people and difficult situations. No one really holds explicit Hinayana tenets today, but the mindset is common.

We hold the Hinayana mindset when we think practice would be easier without all these people, when our solution to delusion is to abandon difficult situations, or when we use practice as an escape from the world. The Mahayana attitude transforms difficulties into the path.

The Mahayana is like building a palace: complicated, time-consuming, but it can host countless beings and lasts forever. The Hinayana is like building a shack: genuine refuge, simpler to build, but it only helps you and isn't sophisticated in the long run. Both are precious — but the Mahayana mindset says: you are an inextricable part of my journey. I can't have a path without all living beings being part of it. I'm building a palace, not a shack.
For further study, Geshe-la explains the types of Hinayana practitioner (returners, once-returners, stream-enterers, etc.) in the first chapters of Ocean of Nectar.
commentary.quote: The Mahayana mindset is: no, you are an inextricable part of my journey, my path. I can't have a path, a journey, without all living beings being part of it. And I'm doing this for all of them.
